> 「若三千大千世界中，所有诸须弥山王，如是等七宝聚，有人持用布施……百分不及一，百千万亿分，乃至算数譬喻所不能及。」

Section twenty-four is a comparison the sutra has made before, escalated once more, and it is worth asking why the same move keeps returning.

The image: every Mount Sumeru in a billion worlds — each one the axis of its world, the tallest thing in its cosmology — heaped with the seven treasures, and given away.

Against: a person who receives four lines of this sutra, holds them, reads them, and explains them to someone else.

Not equal. Not close. A hundredth part does not reach it; no fraction, no analogy, no arithmetic reaches it.

## 须弥山王 is the heaviest object available

Each world has one centre; each centre is a mountain that dwarfs everything else in it. Heap them — all of them, in all the worlds — and the quantity stops being imaginable.

The repetition across sections is not a failure of invention. Each comparison is aimed at a different attachment:

- Section eight compared a cosmic gift against transmission, targeting the notion that merit is a quantity.
- Section eleven multiplied the frame, targeting the notion that a large enough quantity could win.
- Section fifteen stretched it in time, targeting the notion that endurance earns.
- Here, the target is subtler: the notion that the comparison itself is a rule — that one can now calculate which activity yields more.

The sutra escalates until the calculation stops being possible, and then escalates again.

## 百分不及一 is a refusal of proportion

The phrase is deliberately non-numerical. A hundredth part does not reach it; a hundred billionth does not; and then the text abandons counting altogether.

The book's note: this is 极言 — speech pushed to its limit — not a precise ratio. Anyone who tries to compute the exchange rate has already misunderstood which two things are being compared.

## What is being compared

Not "reading beats donating". Not "teaching beats feeding people".

What is compared is 有为 and 无为 in the specific sense established earlier: giving that occurs inside the structure of giver, gift, receiver, result — and receiving a teaching whose content is the dissolution of that structure.

The first is good, real, and bounded, because it has a shape. The second has no shape to be bounded by. That is the entire comparison, and it cannot be expressed as a ratio because the two sides do not share a unit.

## 受持读诵，为他人说

Four activities in one line, and the fourth is the one that keeps the other three from becoming private.

Receive; hold; read; explain. The book's gloss on 读诵 is not "recite for merit" but "let the text pass through you repeatedly until it works on you" — the old practice of returning to a text until it stops being information.

And 为他人说: the transmission is part of the holding. A teaching held and never given dies with its holder, which is the one form of loss this sutra treats as serious.

## The test

What would you have to believe about your own practice in order to accept that a person reading four lines to a friend surpasses a cosmos of gold?

Most readers, on contact, produce a reason why the comparison must be metaphorical and therefore not quite serious. That reason is the thing to look at. It is usually a preference for the measurable.
